claims.text: Increasing the relative Hf percentage in HfNbTaTiZr will improve yield strength and hardness.
Hf is a larger-atomic-size constituent whose enrichment increases atomic-size mismatch in this alloy.
Hf enrichment strengthens the alloy by enhancing lattice distortion and solid-solution strengthening.
The initial material is equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr can be processed using mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering.
A combinatorial synthesis approach can be used to determine the effects of systematically changing Hf content.
Hf content should be increased at the expense of one or more other alloying elements.
Keeping processing conditions and oxygen content controlled allows compositional effects to be isolated.
Greater Hf content causes greater atomic-radius mismatch and increased lattice distortion.
Changing Hf content may modify phase stability or grain size.
Increased lattice strain enhances solid-solution strengthening.
Hf enrichment may produce finer microstructural features.
Lattice strain and finer microstructural features impede dislocation motion and increase mechanical performance.
Hf-enriched samples are predicted to have microhardness and yield strength approximately 10–20% above the equiatomic baseline.
Beyond a composition threshold, secondary-phase formation may negate the strengthening benefit.
The beneficial effect is limited by Hf solubility, and excessive Hf may cause unwanted secondary phases or embrittlement.
XRD, SEM, and microhardness testing can characterize phase or microstructural state and hardness in equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
Compression testing can determine how changing Hf content affects yield strength in this alloy.
Failure of Hf-enriched samples to show a statistically significant hardness and yield-strength improvement over the equiatomic control would falsify the hypothesis.
